title: Glucose–heart-rate coupling shifts with diabetes severity
finding: Across 2,280 AI-READI participants, the strength of dynamic coupling between continuous glucose and heart rate changes systematically with diabetes-severity group.
interpretation: Glucose and cardiac-autonomic dynamics are normally synchronized; that synchronization is altered as metabolic disease progresses, consistent with autonomic involvement.
individual_application: Compute a user's glucose–HR coupling from overlapping CGM + wearable windows and track it against their own baseline. A drift away from baseline is a personal early-warning signal worth surfacing.
caveats: Cohort-level association, cross-sectional. For one person, lead with within-person change, not a single cross-sectional value.

title: Coupling features predict insulin-dependent diabetes
finding: Dynamic cross-modal coupling features carry predictive signal for insulin-dependent diabetes beyond static summaries.
interpretation: How systems move together over time encodes metabolic state that single lab values miss.
individual_application: Use coupling features as part of a user's metabolic picture, not just HbA1c or fasting glucose.
caveats: Predictive at cohort level; not a diagnostic for an individual.

title: Coupling links to clinical burden (frailty, allostatic load)
finding: Cross-modal coupling features relate to composite clinical burden — frailty index and allostatic load.
interpretation: Coupling integrity may be a marker of whole-body physiological resilience, not just glycemic control.
individual_application: Frame coupling to the user as a 'resilience' signal; pair it with their composite scores.

title: Loss of glucose complexity predicts burden beyond HbA1c
finding: Reduced glucose signal complexity (multiscale entropy) at the 1–3 hour scale predicts allostatic load over and above HbA1c.
interpretation: A flatter, less complex glucose signal reflects loss of adaptive regulation — information HbA1c alone does not capture.
individual_application: Compute multiscale entropy of a user's CGM; a downward trend vs baseline flags loss of metabolic flexibility.
caveats: Completed analysis with results payload; effect sizes modest. Needs the user's CGM to span enough days.

title: Nocturnal glucose–HR coupling predicts next-day control
finding: Overnight coupling between glucose and heart rate predicts the following day's glycemic control.
interpretation: Sleep-period physiology sets up the next day; nocturnal coupling is an actionable leading indicator.
individual_application: Surface last night's coupling each morning as a 'today's metabolic readiness' read; ties naturally to sleep interventions.
caveats: Requires overlapping overnight CGM + wearable; demonstrated at cohort level.

title: Sleep–wake transition coupling reorganizes more slowly with diabetes
finding: The speed at which cross-modal coupling reorganizes across the sleep–wake transition is a diabetes marker.
interpretation: Healthy physiology re-couples quickly on waking; sluggish reorganization tracks metabolic dysfunction.
individual_application: Measure a user's coupling change around their wake time; slow reorganization vs baseline is a flag and motivates sleep-timing interventions.
caveats: Completed; sleep staging from wearable is approximate vs PSG.

title: The circadian rhythm of coupling flattens with severity
finding: Glucose–HR coupling strength has its own circadian rhythm that flattens as diabetes severity increases.
interpretation: Loss of a day–night swing in coupling mirrors broader circadian disruption in metabolic disease.
individual_application: Fit a daily rhythm to the user's coupling; a flattening amplitude vs baseline is a personal circadian-health signal.

title: Synchronized multimodal physiology is real and decays with time
finding: A window-level JEPA shows aligned person-time windows are far more predictable than wrong-day or shuffled-participant controls, across four horizons and 36 runs; predictability decays as the horizon lengthens.
interpretation: There is genuine cross-modal temporal coupling in a person's streams — not an artifact — and its reach is finite.
individual_application: Run the frozen JEPA encoder on a user's aligned streams to produce a personal coupling embedding and detect degraded coupling vs their baseline.
caveats: Validated as representation learning; per-individual coupling-degradation scoring is the application direction, not yet clinically validated.

title: Static per-organ aging clocks discriminate diabetes poorly
finding: Static per-organ aging clocks discriminate diabetes severity poorly; in sequence JEPA, static phenotype (retinal/ECG/clinical) dominates age/severity prediction while temporal sequences add little for those endpoints.
interpretation: For coarse endpoints, static snapshots are strong — but the *dynamic* coupling signal is where the novel, actionable physiology lives.
individual_application: Use static clocks for orientation/percentile, but lead the user experience with dynamic coupling and within-person change.
caveats: Motivates the product's emphasis on dynamics over static clocks.

title: Coupling does NOT predict retinal/cardiac structural damage (refuted)
finding: The hypothesis that coupling features predict retinal/cardiac structural damage was refuted in the cohort.
interpretation: Coupling reflects functional/autonomic state, not structural organ damage — a useful boundary on what to claim.
individual_application: Do not tell users their coupling reflects eye or heart structural damage. Keep coupling framed as functional dynamics.
caveats: Included deliberately: the system records and respects negative evidence.
